title: Sandwich Day

jokes.text: Hillary Clinton is president, sir! I thought I would just try to scare you out of it.
jokes.setup: Jack is in a coma and someone is trying to wake him with alarming news
jokes.punchline: The 'alarming news' is revealed to be a deliberate fake-out — and Hillary Clinton as president is the scary scenario
jokes.explanation: Sharp opener that simultaneously establishes Jack's politics, his coma, and the absurdity of the situation. The Hillary Clinton line is perfectly calibrated for the character — Jack would consider this a nightmare. The reveal that it was a deliberate scare tactic adds a second layer. Well-structured with excellent character integration.

jokes.text: This morning, I had to cut my own cantaloupe.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing the indignities of being stripped of his executive power
jokes.punchline: The most profound indignity he can name is cutting his own fruit — treating a basic life task as catastrophic
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect encapsulation of Jack Donaghy's character. The specificity of 'cantaloupe' (not just 'fruit') and the deadpan delivery of this as a genuine crisis reveals everything about how pampered and entitled he is. Highly quotable, extremely economical, and only Jack Donaghy could deliver this line with full sincerity. Strong 8+ justified.

jokes.text: They're moving me from the 52nd floor down to my new office... on 12. 12! You've got to wake up, please!
jokes.setup: Jack being demoted from the 52nd floor
jokes.punchline: The horror of being moved to floor 12 is delivered with such theatrical devastation that it becomes an escalating comedy beat, followed by desperate pleading
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Twelve!' beats work as escalation comedy — the repetition signals that this number is meant to be read as catastrophically low. Solid character work, though slightly less economical than the cantaloupe joke.

jokes.text: Marcus Schenkenberg was there. Who? Okay, the craziest thing happened...
jokes.setup: Liz apparently starts to tell a dream story that begins with 'Marcus Schenkenberg was there'
jokes.punchline: Pete's blank 'Who?' dismisses the famous supermodel entirely, and Liz immediately pivots away from the dream to the Floyd story — the whole dream tangent is dropped as irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Quick throwaway that establishes Liz's nerd/dork persona — she's dreaming about a male supermodel but Pete has no idea who he is, deflating it. Economical but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: You were using your treadmill? Yes, and, yes, Pete, I use it every day.
jokes.setup: Liz mentions she was on her treadmill when Floyd called
jokes.punchline: Pete's incredulous follow-up question implies he doesn't believe she actually uses it, and Liz's defensive over-explanation ('yes, and YES, Pete') confirms she's lying
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that efficiently establishes Liz's self-deception. The structure is clean: Pete's one-word interrogation lands, Liz's protest is clearly a lie, and the audience gets to feel smart for catching it. Good economy.

jokes.text: JetFun. Is that the one with the footbaths? Oh, no, that's AirBike. They also have in-flight pornos and NBC news. JetFun's the one that hands out fresh popcorn.
jokes.setup: Pete asks about JetFun airline
jokes.punchline: The exchange establishes a world of completely absurd budget airlines with bizarre amenities — footbaths, in-flight pornos, NBC news (lumped in with pornos as an equally questionable offering), and fresh popcorn
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock absurdism — the joke creates an entire fictional universe of weird airlines with total confidence. The NBC self-deprecation (NBC news lumped alongside in-flight pornos as equally disreputable) is the sharpest element and the most original beat. The specificity of 'fresh popcorn' as JetFun's distinguishing feature is perfectly ridiculous.

jokes.text: The last time I tried to get in touch with him, some Rust Belt tramp answered the phone.
jokes.setup: Liz explaining why she hasn't been in touch with Floyd
jokes.punchline: 'Rust Belt tramp' is a hilariously specific and snobby geographic insult that reveals Liz's petty jealousy while also being a funny turn of phrase
jokes.explanation: Great phrase — the specificity of 'Rust Belt' elevates what could be a generic insult into something more vivid and geographically comic. It also sets up the running Cleveland joke thread throughout the episode.

jokes.text: I want to be top dog for once instead of just... dog.
jokes.setup: Liz wants to impress Floyd and not be the pathetic one
jokes.punchline: The self-deprecating completion of the metaphor — she doesn't even claim to be a bottom dog, just 'dog' — is perfectly bleak and self-aware
jokes.explanation: Elegantly simple joke that lands through economy and structure. The pause before 'dog' is perfectly placed. This is characteristically Liz — she can't even claim to be 'bottom dog.' The comedy is in the downgrade from the already-low metaphor. Highly quotable, very well constructed.

jokes.text: For once, I am not gonna be Jan Brady. I'm gonna be Marcia, damn it. Oh, my nose! My bad! See? It's starting already.
jokes.setup: Liz declares she's going to be confident like Marcia Brady instead of dorky Jan
jokes.punchline: She immediately injures herself the way Marcia did in the iconic Brady Bunch football episode, undercutting her own declaration in real time
jokes.explanation: Textbook 30 Rock structure: character makes aspirational declaration, reality immediately contradicts it. The Brady Bunch reference is deployed with precision — not just a name-drop but an active callback to a specific moment from the show. The 'See? It's starting already' self-commentary is a nice final beat.

jokes.text: Look out, Floyd. There is a new Liz and... Ooh, Sandwich Day.
jokes.setup: Liz is in the middle of a triumphant declaration about reinventing herself for Floyd
jokes.punchline: The declaration is completely abandoned mid-sentence when she notices Sandwich Day — perfectly illustrating that food trumps all self-improvement for Liz
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon beat. The mid-sentence derailment by food is extremely character-specific and economical. It doesn't need a punchline — the interruption IS the punchline. This kind of joke only works because the character's food obsession is so established, and it pays off beautifully here. Strong 8 justified.

jokes.text: No one knows what it's called or where it is. It's a Teamster secret. But they buy us these sandwiches. Oh, such sandwiches! And the dipping sauce. Oh, joy! God bless us, every one!
jokes.setup: Explaining the mythology of Sandwich Day
jokes.punchline: The escalating reverence — 'Oh, such sandwiches!', 'Oh, joy!', and culminating in a Dickensian 'God bless us, every one!' — treats a free work sandwich with the gravity of a religious miracle
jokes.explanation: The Dickens quote as the punchline ('God bless us, every one') is a genuinely funny escalation of the sandwich reverence. The mystery/secrecy element also sets up the entire B-plot. Strong character work — Liz's food obsession played at maximum absurdity.

jokes.text: By the way, you know who hates unicorns? Mark Wahlberg.
jokes.setup: Jack is departing from Kathy Geiss's office after wishing her well
jokes.punchline: A completely non-sequitur fact about Mark Wahlberg hating unicorns — delivered as a casual aside that makes no sense in context
jokes.explanation: Brilliant non-sequitur. The specificity of Mark Wahlberg + unicorns is maximally absurd, and the casual delivery ('by the way') as if this is relevant information makes it funnier. Also possibly a plant for the Mark Wahlberg running joke in 30 Rock. Maximum economy — five words deliver the punchline. High quotability.

jokes.text: I've been sleeping with the Cindy Crawford of corporations for the last 22 years. What am I supposed to do? Just lie down with some skank like 3M?
jokes.setup: Jack is discussing his options now that he's been pushed out of GE
jokes.punchline: He frames corporate loyalty as a sexual relationship — GE is Cindy Crawford, and going to 3M would be settling for a 'skank.' The specificity of '3M' as the lesser company is perfectly chosen.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The metaphor of corporate loyalty as a romantic/sexual relationship is original and perfectly aligned with Jack's character — he genuinely thinks of GE the way other men think of women. The choice of 3M as the 'skank' alternative is inspired (mundane office supplies brand vs. glamorous GE). 'Cindy Crawford of corporations' is quotable. Strong 8 justified.

jokes.text: Bush? Has it gotten that bad? Good God, I'd rather work for an American car company than jump on that sinking ship.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Jack could go work in the Bush Administration
jokes.punchline: Jack — a Republican — considers the Bush Administration too much of a failure to attach himself to, preferring even the struggling American auto industry
jokes.explanation: Good political joke with strong character integration — Jack is a Bush-era Republican who nevertheless recognizes the administration is collapsing. The American car company comparison doubles the joke. Politically topical for 2008.

jokes.text: Jonathan playing 'I Will Remember You' on a recorder as Jack walks away
jokes.setup: Jack is leaving for his humiliating new office on floor 12; Jonathan is devastated by his boss's demotion
jokes.punchline: Jonathan performs a mournful farewell song on a recorder — an achingly dorky instrument — as if Jack is dying rather than just changing floors
jokes.explanation: Perfectly absurd visual gag. The recorder (children's instrument) makes the moment both more pathetic and funnier. Jonathan's overwrought devotion to Jack played through the most undignified instrument possible. The song choice ('I Will Remember You') adds a layer of earnest tragedy to the comedy.

jokes.text: Everything's great. Yeah, I'm really... crushing it.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if everything is okay after Jack clearly just tried to secretly ride the elevator to floor 12
jokes.punchline: Jack's hollow 'crushing it' after being caught mid-cover-up is maximally ironic — he is demonstrably not crushing it
jokes.explanation: Competent irony beat — the gap between Jack's bravado and his reality is clear. Not as sharp as the cantaloupe or 3M jokes but functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Why are you going to 12? 12? Did I hit 12? I wanted, uh... 4012, which is 52, where I work. Business.
jokes.setup: Jack is caught in the elevator obviously going to floor 12
jokes.punchline: His improvised excuse — '4012, which is 52, where I work' — is transparently nonsensical, and the single word 'Business.' as a conversation-ender is the cherry on top
jokes.explanation: The single-word 'Business.' as an authoritative non-explanation is inspired. Jack's panicked math ('4012, which is 52') is funny in its transparent absurdity, and the smash-cut punctuation of 'Business.' is the real punchline. Very quotable.

jokes.text: You're savoring it? What, you think you're better than us?
jokes.setup: Lutz is eating his sandwich slowly
jokes.punchline: Eating slowly being interpreted as elitist/condescending — the writers'-room guys treat sandwich consumption as a matter of moral character
jokes.explanation: Quick funny beat — treating the act of savoring food as a class crime. Works in the context of the show's food-obsession theme.

jokes.text: Look. Liz Lemon's sandwich is still on her desk. / Ohh. Taking Liz's food is not good. / Where's my mac and cheese?! / But as far as Liz Lemon knows, her sandwich never came.
jokes.setup: Liz's sandwich is unattended; the writers know better than to touch it (established by her mac and cheese history)
jokes.punchline: They steal it anyway, the callback to 'Where's my mac and cheese?!' confirms Liz's food rage is legendary, and the final conspiratorial 'she never knew' is the cover-up beat
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the sandwich plot. The mac and cheese callback efficiently establishes Liz's food rage mythology. The conspiracy framing ('as far as Liz Lemon knows') gives the scene a fun heist-style energy.

jokes.text: I'm pretty tired from playing as hard as I work. Okay, now... bring up 23. And give me some air.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to play it cool and impressive for Floyd; she's claimed to be working hard and playing hard
jokes.punchline: She immediately undercuts herself by asking someone off-screen to 'bring up 23' and 'give me some air' — implying she's completely out of breath and has apparently been doing something strenuous as a performance
jokes.explanation: Funny visual implication — Liz has clearly orchestrated some fake-impressive scenario that she can't sustain. The 'bring up 23' sounds like a sports/workout context. Good character joke about Liz's failed attempts at seeming cool.

jokes.text: Hey, can I take you out to dinner tonight? You know, maybe we hit that barbecue place you puked at. You'll have to be more specific.
jokes.setup: Floyd invites Liz to dinner at a specific memorable restaurant
jokes.punchline: 'You'll have to be more specific' — implying Liz has puked at multiple barbecue places, which is both disgusting and perfectly Liz
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Four words — 'you'll have to be more specific' — communicate an entire history of Liz's relationship with food and her own body. The implication that there are multiple barbecue restaurants she's vomited at is both horrifying and completely in character. Perfect economy, high quotability. Strong 8+ justified.

jokes.text: Oh, somebody get me out of this dress! I can't breathe!
jokes.setup: Liz presumably changed into an impressive outfit to greet Floyd
jokes.punchline: The moment Floyd leaves she immediately starts screaming to be freed from the dress — it's purely performative, uncomfortable, and she can't wait to escape it
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Liz's performance of femininity is immediately shed when no longer needed. Funny implied visual of Liz gasping for air in a too-tight dress.

jokes.text: Huh. You guys are working hard for once.
jokes.setup: The writers are huddled over Liz's desk doing something suspicious (stealing her sandwich)
jokes.punchline: Liz misreads conspiratorial sandwich theft as actual productivity and compliments them for it
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony beat — the audience knows what's happening and Liz doesn't. Economical and serves the plot.

jokes.text: This is all my fault, Miss Lemon, because I let it happen, and the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing. Please ask my permission before you quote me, Kenneth.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is confessing responsibility for the sandwich theft, quoting Edmund Burke
jokes.punchline: Liz responds as if she is in fact Edmund Burke — 'Please ask my permission before you quote me, Kenneth' — delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Liz's response implies she believes herself to be the originator of the Edmund Burke quote, delivered with absolute authority. This is exceptional because: (1) it's completely character-specific — only Liz's combination of obliviousness and ego produces this, (2) the structure is flawless — the setup leads you to expect anger about the sandwich, and the punchline goes somewhere completely unexpected, (3) it's wildly quotable, (4) maximum economy. This is comfortably in the 8+ tier.

jokes.text: I don't know how, but you're gonna get me another sandwich, or I'm gonna cut your face up so bad, you'll have a chin. You'll all have chins!
jokes.setup: Liz discovers her sandwich has been stolen and threatens the writers
jokes.punchline: 'You'll have a chin' as a threat is wonderfully specific and bizarre — giving someone a chin is not normally a threat, but in Liz's food-rage state, physical alteration is the most menacing thing she can think of
jokes.explanation: A genuinely classic 30 Rock threat. 'I'm gonna cut your face so bad you'll have a chin' subverts the standard threat structure in a completely unexpected direction — a chin is a cosmetic addition, not a wound, making the threat absurd rather than violent. 'You'll all have chins!' as a follow-up escalation is perfect. Extremely quotable. Strong 8 justified.

jokes.text: The elevator door closes on Jack. He reads the floor indicator. It says 'Failure.'
jokes.setup: Jack is descending to floor 12 in the elevator
jokes.punchline: The floor indicator reads 'Failure' instead of a number — a surreal visual gag that externalizes Jack's emotional state as literal elevator signage
jokes.explanation: Exceptional visual gag. The show literalizes Jack's internal state through the elevator display — 'Failure' as his destination. Pure visual comedy that requires no dialogue. The economy is perfect (one word), the absurdism is calibrated, and it's deeply character-specific. This is top-tier 30 Rock visual comedy. Strong 8 justified.

jokes.text: Wow, snow in May. Thank you, global warming, for extreme, unpredictable weather patterns.
jokes.setup: There's unseasonable snow in May
jokes.punchline: Thanking global warming with mock gratitude for the cold weather — the irony being that global warming is causing both extremes
jokes.explanation: Functional but relatively generic environmental joke. The show does this kind of topical satirical aside competently but without exceptional craft. Not character-specific to Floyd particularly.

jokes.text: There was actually a tornado in Cleveland last week. Destroyed an entire city block... three bowling alleys, a liquor store, and the liquor-store museum.
jokes.setup: Floyd mentions a tornado hit Cleveland
jokes.punchline: The destroyed block contains a 'liquor-store museum' — implying Cleveland's cultural institutions include a museum dedicated to liquor stores, which is both a Cleveland joke and an absurdist invention
jokes.explanation: The 'liquor-store museum' is a brilliant invention. The joke earns its laugh through specificity — three bowling alleys, a liquor store, AND the liquor-store museum. The escalation from liquor store to liquor-store museum (a museum dedicated to liquor stores) perfectly captures the running Cleveland-as-depressed-rust-belt-city theme. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Yikes! Do you know it is 4:30? I haven't stayed up this late since college. And behind this trapdoor, more Orcs.
jokes.setup: Liz and Floyd are clearly having a great time; she says she hasn't been up this late since college
jokes.punchline: The college reference implies studying or partying, but she's apparently been playing Dungeons & Dragons or similar fantasy game ('more Orcs')
jokes.explanation: Great Liz Lemon joke — the 'more Orcs' reveal subverts expectations about what kind of fun they're having. It's perfectly in character that Liz's idea of a great night with a guy is tabletop gaming. The timing of the reveal is clean.

jokes.text: This smells just like Hill People Milk. I've been drinking this since I was a baby!
jokes.setup: Kenneth smells the Teamsters' moonshine/alcohol at the drinking contest
jokes.punchline: Kenneth identifies it as 'Hill People Milk' — implying he was raised on moonshine from birth, which is both a dark joke about his rural upbringing and the setup for his ability to outdrink everyone
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'Hill People Milk' is inspired — it's a folksy, disturbing euphemism for moonshine that tells you everything about Kenneth's Appalachian upbringing in one invented phrase. The fact that he's been drinking it since infancy is darkly funny and explains his tolerance. Only Kenneth could deliver this. Strong 8 justified.

jokes.text: Like right now, for instance. Well, what does New York have that Cleveland doesn't have? I read that you guys are getting an Ikea. Yeah, I'll believe it when I see it. We've just been burned before.
jokes.setup: Floyd says he regrets leaving New York; Liz challenges what New York has that Cleveland doesn't
jokes.punchline: The debate about New York vs Cleveland is resolved through the Ikea — and Floyd's weary 'we've just been burned before' treats the absence of Ikea as a source of genuine civic trauma
jokes.explanation: The Ikea-as-Cleveland's-great-civic-aspiration is funny and the 'burned before' delivery gives it pathos. Sets up the Ikea callback in the climax. Good running gag infrastructure.

jokes.text: Now turn and look back at me. / Attaboy. Eat it up, Cleveland.
jokes.setup: Floyd has said goodbye and is walking away
jokes.punchline: Liz stage-directs his departure like a movie scene she's choreographed in her head, then gloats to an imaginary Cleveland audience — revealing she's been performing this whole time
jokes.explanation: Reveals Liz's entire cool-girl performance as a consciously constructed tableau. 'Attaboy. Eat it up, Cleveland' is a great line — she's gloating to Cleveland as an abstraction. The stage-direction framing ('Now turn and look back at me') is perfectly absurd. Strong character moment.

jokes.text: I even stopped to catch a snowflake with my tongue, but, evidently, that's some sort of signal in Chelsea.
jokes.setup: Jack is wandering the streets in existential crisis, trying to connect with life
jokes.punchline: The innocent childhood act of catching snowflakes has a gay cruising interpretation in Chelsea (Manhattan's historically gay neighborhood), and Jack's oblivious discovery of this is the joke
jokes.explanation: Elegantly constructed joke. The setup (Jack having an existential walk) leads to an innocent act (catching snowflakes) that lands him in an unexpected context (Chelsea cruising). The economy is excellent — 'evidently' does a lot of work, implying he found out the hard way. Jack's complete obliviousness is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I was hit by lightning as a child. They made a movie about me.
jokes.setup: Jack asks what happened to someone's voice (it's changed)
jokes.punchline: The lightning explanation is already absurd, but 'They made a movie about me' is a perfect non-sequitur escalation delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A great one-off absurdist joke. The movie detail adds nothing logically but everything comedically — it implies a grandiosity to the lightning injury that is completely unearned and funny. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: You have to leave GE. / What did you say? / Geriatric Extended Care. That's what this wing of the hospital is called.
jokes.setup: Jack hears 'You have to leave GE' and takes it as divine/coma-patient guidance to leave General Electric
jokes.punchline: GE means 'Geriatric Extended Care' — the 'sign' Jack received was just a hospital staffer enforcing visiting hours
jokes.explanation: Classic double-meaning structure executed well. The GE/Geriatric Extended Care coincidence is a clean misdirection payoff. The joke works on two levels: it's funny that Jack desperately wants a sign, and funnier that the 'sign' is just mundane hospital bureaucracy. Good structure justifies the 8.

jokes.text: The poor guy got Lemoned... hard.
jokes.setup: Liz reports that Floyd was upset about leaving New York after their night together
jokes.punchline: 'Lemoned' as a verb meaning 'subjected to Liz Lemon's particular brand of romantic chaos' — a meta-acknowledgment that Liz is a force of romantic destruction
jokes.explanation: Turning a character's last name into a verb describing her specific pathology is exceptional character comedy. 'Lemoned' implies a whole taxonomy of romantic disaster that is uniquely Liz. 'Hard' intensifies it perfectly. This is the kind of word invention that can become part of a show's vocabulary. Extremely quotable and deeply character-specific. Easily an 8+.

jokes.text: No, Jenna, I did not come back from the bathroom and hand him my underwear. That's how I met that mobster.
jokes.setup: Jenna apparently has a technique for seducing men involving handing them underwear from the bathroom
jokes.punchline: The mundane (to Jenna) revelation that this technique once connected her with a mobster, delivered as if this is a normal story
jokes.explanation: Strong Jenna character joke. The underwear-handing technique is gross enough, but the casual mobster disclosure is perfect — it's delivered as a practical anecdote, not a cautionary tale, which tells you everything about Jenna's life. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Now, you two, kiss. You with the sport coat, you're the girl.
jokes.setup: Jenna and a crew member are trying to negotiate with the Teamsters for the sandwich location
jokes.punchline: The Teamster responds to their pitch by demanding they kiss — and assigns gender roles based on the sport coat
jokes.explanation: Funny Teamster intimidation bit. The logic of 'sport coat = girl' is absurd and confident. Establishes the Teamsters as a chaotic, unpredictable force.

jokes.text: I know what driving the long haul's like. After my junior year at Oberlin, we road-tripped to South by Southwest. You lads got a lot of nerve.
jokes.setup: Jenna is trying to connect with the Teamsters by claiming working-class solidarity
jokes.punchline: Her 'long haul' experience is a road trip from Oberlin (elite liberal arts college) to Austin for a music festival — the exact opposite of Teamster experience
jokes.explanation: Good joke about class cluelessness. Oberlin + South by Southwest is the perfect upper-middle-class-person-pretending-to-be-working-class combo. The Teamster's contemptuous 'lot of nerve' response is well-earned.

jokes.text: Bible trivia? Drinking contest. Here. Tonight.
jokes.setup: The crew suggests bible trivia as a competition for the sandwich location
jokes.punchline: The Teamster rejects bible trivia in favor of a drinking contest with complete authority — the subversion of the religious option for the more dissolute one
jokes.explanation: Punchy and economical. The Teamster's three-word response (after the setup of 'Bible trivia?') is confident and funny. Sets up the drinking contest plot.

jokes.text: Uh, a Band-Aid just fell out of your hair.
jokes.setup: A Teamster is hosting them in what is apparently a squalid venue
jokes.punchline: A Band-Aid falls out of the Teamster's hair — a deeply unsanitary and absurd detail delivered as casual observation
jokes.explanation: Quick gross visual gag. The casual delivery of 'a Band-Aid just fell out of your hair' is more funny than any elaboration would be. Good economy.

jokes.text: Wait, wait, wait. One storm? That's all it takes? We're still gonna make popcorn. Just no more airplanes.
jokes.setup: JetFun airline has cancelled all flights due to the storm — and apparently shut down entirely as an airline
jokes.punchline: The airline employee's calm pivot to 'we'll still make popcorn, just no more airplanes' — one storm destroys the whole airline, but the popcorn mission continues
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to the absurd airline worldbuilding from earlier. JetFun defined itself by popcorn, so naturally when the airline folds, the popcorn survives. The logic is internally consistent in an absurd way. 'Just no more airplanes' is delivered with perfect resignation.

jokes.text: Who was that bitch that answered your phone eight months ago?
jokes.setup: Floyd shows up unexpectedly at Liz's apartment; she goes immediately for the thing she's been holding for eight months
jokes.punchline: No preamble, no reestablishment of rapport — she goes directly for the jugular with 'who was that bitch'
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Liz's pent-up jealousy erupting immediately. The directness is funny in context.

jokes.text: What's her lower-back tattoo? A Chinese character that she thinks means 'peace,' but it really means 'I have chlamydia'?
jokes.setup: Liz is building a profile of the woman who answered Floyd's phone
jokes.punchline: The tattoo joke subverts the 'mistranslated tattoo' cliché by giving it a medically specific punchline — not just 'something rude' but specifically chlamydia
jokes.explanation: Takes a well-worn joke structure (mistranslated tattoo) and elevates it with specificity. 'Chlamydia' as the actual meaning is funnier than a generic insult because it's medical and specific.

jokes.text: Drinking's against my beliefs, like gambling or freeway driving.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is asked why he can't participate in the drinking contest
jokes.punchline: He lists three moral prohibitions: drinking, gambling, and 'freeway driving' — the last one is a completely unexpected addition that suggests a religious/rural worldview where high-speed roads are sinful
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The list of Kenneth's prohibitions is almost right (drinking, gambling are classic religious prohibitions) and then 'freeway driving' is an inspired addition that is specific to Kenneth's Appalachian/backwoods character. It suggests a whole religious community that has never needed an interstate. The joke is maximally economical and could only come from Kenneth. Strong 8+ fully justified.

jokes.text: This is more important than me getting home or my partner meeting with Peter Venkman.
jokes.setup: Floyd says this is more important than a business meeting
jokes.punchline: Peter Venkman is a Ghostbusters character — which Liz will call out later
jokes.explanation: Functions as both a joke on its own (eagle-eyed viewers will catch it) and a setup for the callback payoff later. Good plant — specific enough to be noticeable.

jokes.text: And I can't drink! I still got my Hollywood sock on.
jokes.setup: Characters are listing reasons why they can't drink against the Teamsters
jokes.punchline: 'Hollywood sock' is an invented medical term that apparently prevents drinking — the specificity of 'Hollywood' makes it funnier as an unexplained absurdism
jokes.explanation: 'Hollywood sock' is a great throwaway — it sounds medical but is clearly invented. The unexplained specificity is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: And I can't have booze because I'm on antibiotics after having some skanky club sex. He's on antibiotics because he lost his lucky penny and assumed it fell in his ear again.
jokes.setup: Frank says he can't drink because of antibiotics from 'skanky club sex'
jokes.punchline: Lutz reveals Frank's actual reason: he lost a penny and thought it went in his ear again — suggesting this is a recurring problem — which is both more disgusting and more absurd than the original explanation
jokes.explanation: Two-stage joke: the 'skanky club sex' setup is already funny, but the real reason (penny in ear, apparently not for the first time) is better. 'Again' does a tremendous amount of work. The escalation structure is clean and surprising.

jokes.text: Shut up, Lutz. Your surgery was for an undescended testicle. Wrong again. It was for two undescended testicles.
jokes.setup: Frank exposes Lutz's real surgery; Lutz corrects him
jokes.punchline: Lutz corrects Frank not to deny the undescended testicle but to specify there were TWO — making it worse while somehow asserting this as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in escalation comedy. Frank says 'undescended testicle.' You'd expect Lutz to deny it. Instead he corrects the NUMBER upward. 'Wrong again. It was for two undescended testicles' delivered with dignity is a perfect subversion. The 'Wrong again' implies Frank has been wrong about Lutz's medical history before. Exceptional structure — this is comparable to the 'Snip snap' anchor example in its use of correction-as-escalation.

jokes.text: I'll do it, but only for the attention.
jokes.setup: No one can participate in the drinking contest; Jenna volunteers
jokes.punchline: Jenna's motivation is pure narcissism — 'only for the attention' — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is a reasonable and obvious explanation
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly encapsulate Jenna Maroney's entire character. The joke works because (1) it's the most honest thing Jenna has ever said about herself, (2) 'only for the attention' is a socially unacceptable motivation that she states with zero shame, (3) it gets a 'Yes!' reaction as if it's a perfectly valid reason. Maximum economy, maximum character integration. Top-tier joke.

jokes.text: It's in their contract.
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Jack can make the Teamsters reveal the sandwich location only if they lose a drinking contest
jokes.punchline: Jack confirms it as a contractual requirement — treating the absurd Teamster drinking-contest clause as a mundane labor negotiation item
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan line. Jack's 'It's in their contract' treats the most absurd premise as boring bureaucratic fact. The joke is entirely in the delivery context — three words spoken with complete authority make the Teamster clause seem like a standard labor provision. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: I'm a bitch, I'm a lover? I'm a child, I'm a... Mother!
jokes.setup: Jack is apparently humming/quoting the Meredith Brooks song 'Bitch' to himself; Liz completes the lyric
jokes.punchline: The absurd image of Jack Donaghy singing 'Bitch' by Meredith Brooks is followed by Liz instinctively completing the lyric, revealing she knows it perfectly
jokes.explanation: Funny absurdist moment — Jack Donaghy singing Meredith Brooks is inherently comic. Liz's automatic completion of the lyric adds a character beat about her musical taste.

jokes.text: I'm so glad you're bringing this up. Really? You are? / I didn't bring it up last night because we were having so much fun... Floyd then reveals his phone was never dead and the email about a flight was fake.
jokes.setup: Liz works up the courage to confront Floyd about the girl; Floyd seems surprisingly receptive
jokes.punchline: Floyd's eagerness to talk is revealed as a stalling tactic — his phone wasn't dead, the email was fake, he invented a flight to avoid the conversation
jokes.explanation: Good cringe reveal — Floyd's 'I'm so glad you're bringing this up' is fake-out enthusiasm. The escalating deceptions (dead phone, fake email, invented flight) work as comic reveals.

jokes.text: Peter Venkman... That's from Ghostbusters! You used Ghostbusters for evil!
jokes.setup: Floyd used 'my partner meeting with Peter Venkman' as an excuse to rush off; Liz realizes Peter Venkman is a Ghostbusters character
jokes.punchline: 'You used Ghostbusters for evil!' — Liz is more outraged by the desecration of the IP than by the lie itself
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. Liz's moral hierarchy — 'using Ghostbusters for evil' framed as worse than the lying itself — is pure character comedy. The outrage at the misuse of a beloved property over the actual deception is perfectly Liz Lemon. 'You used Ghostbusters for evil!' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode. Strong 8 fully justified.

jokes.text: I'm single. I'm a lawyer. I wear nice coats. I'm the Michael Clayton of Cleveland.
jokes.setup: Floyd is arguing that he's doing fine and Liz should have come to Cleveland
jokes.punchline: 'The Michael Clayton of Cleveland' — Michael Clayton is a prestige legal thriller; Floyd is claiming its status while rooting it in Cleveland, which deflates it
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-sell (single, lawyer, nice coats) before landing on 'Michael Clayton of Cleveland' is well-constructed. The Cleveland qualifier is what makes it funny — it's a local version of prestige. Also a contemporary film reference that lands in 2008.

jokes.text: Well, I hope your car blows up.
jokes.setup: Floyd made his 'Michael Clayton' speech; Liz responds
jokes.punchline: Liz's response is 'I hope your car blows up' — a reference to the Michael Clayton plot (his car does blow up) that also serves as a genuine angry wish
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback/film reference. 'I hope your car blows up' works on two levels: it's a genuine curse from Liz, AND it's a specific Michael Clayton plot reference (his car is bombed). The economy is exceptional — five words do double duty. Very quotable and has rewatch value for viewers who catch the movie reference.

jokes.text: I'll move to Cleveland when you get that Ikea. Never! Oh, you... Don't you deprive the good people of Cleveland an Ikea! You are vindictive, Liz Lemon!
jokes.setup: Liz and Floyd are fighting; she threatens to withhold the Ikea
jokes.punchline: Liz's threat is to somehow deny Cleveland its Ikea — and Floyd's 'don't you deprive the good people of Cleveland an Ikea!' treats this as a genuine civic threat
jokes.explanation: The Ikea callback pays off magnificently. 'Don't you deprive the good people of Cleveland an Ikea!' is a genuinely great line — the idea that Liz has the power to withhold the Ikea from Cleveland and would use this as a weapon is absurdist escalation at its best. The callback to the earlier 'we've been burned before' makes this richer. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, come on, you guys. You guys do one. I've had 10 shots. You've only had five shots. No, today. I've had 10 shots today.
jokes.setup: Jenna is losing the drinking contest and asking for help
jokes.punchline: She clarifies she's had 10 shots 'today' — meaning five were before the contest, as a baseline
jokes.explanation: Good Jenna character joke — the 'no, TODAY' correction implies she arrived pre-loaded. Works as character building for Jenna's alcoholism.

jokes.text: Battery's dead. I got a half-hour before they track me down. Alcohol? This smells just like Hill People Milk. I've been drinking this since I was a baby! Mmm! It's on, y'all.
jokes.setup: Kenneth said drinking is against his beliefs; his pager/battery dies, freeing him from institutional oversight for 30 minutes
jokes.punchline: Once free from surveillance, Kenneth immediately embraces the moonshine using the 'Hill People Milk' callback — and transforms into a confident drinker ('It's on, y'all')
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff for multiple setups. The battery dying as the liberating event is a nice structural device. The 'Hill People Milk' callback lands perfectly, and Kenneth's transformation into a confident drinker ('It's on, y'all') is a great character reveal. The 30-minute window of freedom adds a funny constraint.

jokes.text: How'd they do that? [Kenneth is apparently winning/dominating the drinking contest — visual reaction beat from the Teamsters]
jokes.setup: The Teamsters expected to easily beat the NBC staff
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, the teetotaling page from rural Appalachia, is apparently destroying them
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Hill People Milk setup. Kenneth's capacity is the natural result of a childhood of unwitting alcohol consumption. The Teamsters' stunned reaction ('How'd they do that?') is the right note of disbelief.

jokes.text: I'll be here? In sunshine or in shadow?
jokes.setup: Jonathan has been playing recorder throughout the episode; now he's playing 'Danny Boy' presumably outside the Teamster bar
jokes.punchline: Jonathan has apparently followed Jack (or found a new venue for his devotional recorder playing) — the callback to the recorder joke in a new context
jokes.explanation: Second appearance of Jonathan's recorder as a running gag. The 'Danny Boy' selection is appropriate for the Irish-Teamster context, adding a layer. Running gag maintained well.

jokes.text: You never know when someone's going to slip into a coma and leave you regretting all the things you didn't say or get in writing from the company's lawyers.
jokes.setup: Jack is giving Liz life advice about not letting Floyd get away without resolving things — genuine emotional advice
jokes.punchline: The advice pivots from sincere ('regret the things you didn't say') to Jack-specific ('or get in writing from the company's lawyers') — revealing Jack's emotional advice is always filtered through corporate legalism
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Jack's advice starts as genuine emotional wisdom and is corrupted mid-sentence by his instinct to reference corporate legal documentation. 'Or get in writing from the company's lawyers' is the perfect Jack Donaghy rider to an otherwise sincere moment. The coma setup (Don being in a coma throughout) adds another ironic layer.

jokes.text: What I'm trying to say is you're... young and you still haven't blown it completely, so don't... start now.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to give Liz inspiring advice to go after Floyd
jokes.punchline: Jack's version of encouragement is 'you still haven't blown it completely' — the backhanded nature of the compliment is pure Jack
jokes.explanation: Jack's pep talk as backhanded compliment is perfect character comedy. 'You still haven't blown it completely' is encouraging in the most brutal way possible. The pauses before 'young' and 'start now' imply he's choosing these words as the nicest possible framing.

jokes.text: What's that in your bag? Uh, a sandwich and... dipping sauce. Unh-unh. That's more than 3 ounces. You can't bring that past here.
jokes.setup: Liz is rushing through airport security to catch Floyd
jokes.punchline: The TSA confiscates her Teamster sandwich under liquids rules — the greatest sandwich in the world falls victim to post-9/11 airport security
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — the legendary sandwich meets its end through bureaucratic airport security. The dipping sauce exceeding 3 ounces is a nice specific detail.

jokes.text: That's sort of a cliché. You're sort of a cliché.
jokes.setup: Liz explains she needs to catch a guy before he flies to Cleveland; the TSA agent says that's a cliché
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'You're sort of a cliché' comeback to a TSA agent — a risky and unhinged response to federal security
jokes.explanation: Funny beat — the TSA agent has no business calling out romantic clichés, and Liz's combative return volley is both risky (TSA!) and funny. 'One-way ticket to Montreal? Crazy eyes.' is an additional funny detail.

jokes.text: You're choosing a sandwich over a guy. Hmm. That is less clichéd.
jokes.setup: Liz is forced to choose between leaving the sandwich and catching Floyd
jokes.punchline: The TSA agent's 'That is less clichéd' — delivered apparently as a compliment — when Liz appears to choose the sandwich over the guy
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and character moment. 'That is less clichéd' is a perfect callback to the earlier cliché exchange, and the implication that Liz would prioritize a sandwich over a romantic relationship is very Liz. The TSA agent's approval of the unconventional choice is funny deadpan.

jokes.text: I can do it. I can have it all! [Liz runs while eating the foil-wrapped sandwich at full speed] God, lady, you're eating foil!
jokes.setup: Liz decides to eat the sandwich at the checkpoint rather than leave it behind — while also running to catch Floyd
jokes.punchline: She runs through the airport eating a foil-wrapped sandwich, prompting a horrified bystander to point out she's eating the foil
jokes.explanation: Great physical comedy beat that pays off the whole sandwich/Floyd dilemma. 'I can have it all!' as a feminist declaration applied to sandwich + man is perfectly absurd. The foil detail is the perfect specificity — not just eating the sandwich, but eating the FOIL. Stranger's horrified reaction lands the joke. Strong physical/character comedy.

jokes.text: God, lady, you're eating foil!
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to eat her sandwich before the TSA confiscates it
jokes.punchline: She's eating it so fast she's consuming the foil wrapping
jokes.explanation: A great physical comedy beat. The image of Liz eating foil in her desperation to save the sandwich is perfectly calibrated — she's degrading herself for food, which is her defining characteristic. 'God, lady' is the ideal horrified bystander response.

jokes.text: I don't want your car to explode and I don't want you to go into a coma and I don't want to stab you in the face with a giant fork. What? Oh, that's not you. I've been threatening a lot of people lately.
jokes.setup: Liz has caught Floyd and is explaining why she came to the airport — delivering heartfelt things she doesn't want to happen to him
jokes.punchline: 'I don't want to stab you in the face with a giant fork' is clearly directed at someone else; Liz's 'Oh, that's not you. I've been threatening a lot of people lately' treats this as normal behavior
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The list starts with sincere/movie-callback threats (car explosion, coma) then accidentally includes 'stab you in the face with a giant fork' — which Liz has to clarify is for someone else. 'I've been threatening a lot of people lately' delivered as a casual self-assessment is exceptional. The 'giant fork' specificity is perfect. Very quotable, strong 8+ justified.

jokes.text: And I wolfed my Teamster sub for you. Wait, no. Is that a saying?
jokes.setup: Liz is listing romantic gestures she made — coming to the airport, giving up the sandwich
jokes.punchline: She offers 'I wolfed my Teamster sub for you' as a declaration of devotion, then immediately second-guesses whether this is a recognized romantic idiom
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Liz reframes eating a sandwich quickly as a grand romantic gesture, then acknowledges it might not be standard. The self-interrupting 'Wait, no. Is that a saying?' is funny and self-aware.

jokes.text: MSNBC has confirmed that former GE executive Jack Donaghy will be named by President Bush as the new Homeland Security Director of Crisis and Weather Management.
jokes.setup: Throughout the episode Jack has been in existential crisis about leaving GE; he misread a hospital sign as instructions to 'leave GE'
jokes.punchline: The news reveals Jack IS leaving GE — but to become Bush's new crisis/weather management director, which pays off both the GE plot and the running global warming/weather jokes
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The 'leave GE' sign (actually 'Geriatric Extended Care') turns out to be prophetic anyway — Jack does leave GE. The Bush administration callback is perfect (Jack earlier said he'd rather work for an American car company than Bush, making this funnier). 'Crisis and Weather Management' also pays off the global warming/weather running thread.

jokes.text: MAN ON P.A: Flight 31 to Montreal is now blurghing.
jokes.setup: Airport PA announcements throughout
jokes.punchline: 'Blurghing' is not a word — the PA announcement degenerates into nonsense as the final gag of the episode
jokes.explanation: Funny final non-sequitur. 'Blurghing' as the last word of the episode is a good absurdist capper — meaningless, confident, and funny in its complete arbitrariness.

tmdb_overview: Floyd stays at Liz's place overnight when his flight is canceled. Meanwhile, Jack is demoted to the 12th floor, causing him to question his future status at the company. Finally, the staff celebrates Annual Sandwich Day with mysterious sandwiches from a secret location in Brooklyn.
insight: Absurdist escalation reaches peak density: 2.89 jokes per minute across 56 gags.
